cl_gen_telescoping.q: Do women go from first use to problems faster than men?
cl_gen_telescoping.short: Not shown for women in general. It was seen mostly in people in treatment.
cl_gen_telescoping.but: Every study relied on people remembering ages from years before.
how: The idea came mostly from small groups of people in treatment or in Alcoholics Anonymous, who had to remember years later when each step happened.
In two big US surveys of adults in the general population, women had their first drink later than men, and fewer women than men became dependent on alcohol.
Among people who did become dependent, women got there about as fast as men: about 6 years after their first drink, on average. The survey's authors read their results as men being faster.
A review says a faster course was found mostly in women already in treatment, who may have more severe problems. A US survey about cannabis, described in another paper, found it too.

cl_gen_women_treatment_entry.q: Are women less likely than men to get alcohol or drug treatment?
cl_gen_women_treatment_entry.short: For alcohol, somewhat less likely, mostly years after problems start. For drugs, about the same.
cl_gen_women_treatment_entry.but: The surveys are from the US, and people remembered dates years later.
how: In US surveys from 1991 to 2002, men with alcohol dependence got treatment more often or sooner than women in some age groups. Some studies found that women who did get treatment got there sooner.
In a 1992 survey, as a review describes it, 23 in 100 men and 15 in 100 women with alcohol problems had ever been treated. The gap began 8 or more years after the problems started.
For drug problems, and for treatment in the past year, reviews describe no difference. In 2015, about 10 in 100 women and 11 in 100 men who needed treatment for alcohol or drugs got it.
Women more often went to mental health services. Reviews list barriers such as childcare and fear of losing custody, but several surveys found few differences in the barriers women and men named.

freq.what: women with alcohol problems had ever been treated
freq.note: One US survey, 1991 to 1992, as a review describes it; treatment includes Alcoholics Anonymous.

cl_gen_women_treatment_outcomes.q: Once in treatment, do women do as well as men?
cl_gen_women_treatment_outcomes.short: Most large studies found no difference between women and men once in treatment.
cl_gen_women_treatment_outcomes.but: This comes from two reviews by one research group; we have not read the studies themselves.
how: Two reviews by one research group looked at many studies of people who had already started treatment. They did not check how good the studies were.
In large studies, women and men mostly stayed in treatment about as long and had similar results. Finding no difference does not prove the results are the same.
Where differences appeared, the older review found women mostly did better. The newer one found more cases where women did worse, mainly in quitting smoking and with some medicines.
Women-only programmes gave mixed results. In the one trial that compared results, a women-only programme showed no difference from two mixed ones, and did less well than a costlier hospital one.

_tf.statement: It has been shown that women in general develop alcohol or drug problems faster than men.
A faster course in women was seen mostly in people already in treatment.
For alcohol, the gap in getting treatment showed up mostly years after problems started.
Women with drug problems were much less likely than men to get treatment.
Most large studies found that women do worse than men once in treatment.

_quiz.q: In two big US surveys, people who became dependent on alcohol got there how long after their first drink, on average?
In one 1992 US survey, how many women with alcohol problems had ever been treated?
